title: Free Printable Chore Charts (Every Age, Editable)
meta_description: Free printable chore charts for every age, toddler to teen. Make an editable chart in seconds, with honest tips from a dad of four and foster parent.
h1: Free Printable Chore Charts for Every Age
intro: A chore chart only does its job once it's printed and stuck somewhere your kids actually walk past. That's the whole idea behind this page. Use the picker just below to choose a format and your child's age, and you'll get a free chart you can edit in your browser and print on the spot — no account, no email, no paywall. Underneath the picker is a linked map of every chart we've built, broken out by age and by style, so you can jump straight to the one that fits. I'm Andrew, writing for the SproutChores family. We've got four kids of our own, currently spanning nine to eighteen, and over the years we've also fostered a few little ones who arrived with no routine at all. Across all of that, one thing held true: a sheet of paper taped to the fridge beat anything glowing on a phone, because the kids could see it. So pick a format and an age, print the thing, and read on for how to choose well and how the work should grow up alongside your child.

sections.heading: Why a printed chart beats one buried in an app
sections.body:
We tried to be the modern parents who run everything from a phone. It never stuck, and the reason was simple once we noticed it: an app lives in a grown-up's pocket, where no child ever looks. A chart only changes behavior when the child can glance at it and know what's expected without being told. Paper on the wall does that. A notification does not.

That's why every chart here is built to come off the screen and onto a surface. With younger kids especially, we found it worked best to put each chart right where the work happens rather than collecting everything in one master list by the door. A morning routine belongs near where they get dressed; a kitchen job belongs in the kitchen. The page becomes a quiet reminder of the next step instead of one more thing a parent has to repeat all day.

Printing also makes the chart almost free to restart, which matters more than it sounds. The systems that survive in a real family aren't the elaborate ones — they're the ones you can dust off after a vacation or a chaotic week and pin back up in two minutes. A fancy setup that collapses the first time life gets busy isn't a better system; it's a more fragile one. Cheap, printable, and easy to put back is exactly what you want.

sections.heading: Choosing the right starting point — format first, then age
sections.body:
There are two decisions in the picker, and they're easier when you take them in order. First, the format: a daily grid for routines you want done every single day, a weekly layout for jobs that rotate, a picture-based version for kids who can't read yet, or a reward-style chart if you're building one specific habit. Match the format to the problem you're actually trying to solve, not to whichever looks cutest.

Then the age. The age sets the difficulty, but treat it as a starting line rather than a verdict. If your child has never had real responsibilities, or a previous chart died a quiet death on the fridge, start a notch easier than their age suggests. A child who can succeed at a short list every day will outpace one handed an impressive list they learn to ignore. You can always raise the bar; pulling back from a kid who feels overwhelmed is the harder direction.

We learned this most sharply while fostering. The children who came to us had lived without any predictable rhythm, and for them a small, dependable structure they could count on did far more good than an ambitious one. Once they could trust what came next, the resistance we'd assumed was defiance mostly melted — a lot of it had just been not knowing. The same principle holds for any kid: pick the level they can hit consistently, print it, watch for a week or two, and nudge it upward when the current version starts to feel too easy.

sections.heading: How the work grows up with your child
sections.body:
It helps to picture these charts as rungs on a ladder rather than one fixed list you'll use forever. At the bottom, with toddlers and preschoolers, the chart is really about self-care and routine — getting dressed, brushing teeth, putting their own things away. Don't grade the quality; you'll be redoing most of it. What you're really building is the idea that they're a member of this household with a part to play, plus the muscle memory that makes the bigger jobs feel normal later.

Through the elementary years the ability finally catches up to the expectation, and the charts get meatier: dishes, trash, helping with meals, work in the yard. We don't pay our kids square by square for any of this. The everyday jobs belong to the family, and we say so out loud — the contribution is the point. Allowance does exist in our house, but it rides on the overall picture of effort, reliability, and how a kid carries themselves, not on a per-task tally. We also keep screen time and treats off the chart entirely, so cooperation never curdles into a negotiation.

By the teen years, frankly, a chart on the fridge stops working, and the version we use looks more like a grown-up agreement than a sticker sheet — that lives on the teen-specific page. The deeper reason all of this matters is the reframe we keep coming back to: chores aren't really about getting the house clean. They're rehearsal for running a life. And the chart itself is a tool for us, the parents — a way to see at a glance who's thriving and who needs a hand — not a gadget meant to bribe a kid into helping.

faq.q: Are these chore charts actually free to print?
faq.a: Yes. Every chart on this page is free to make, edit, and print — there's no account to create, no email to hand over, and nothing locked behind a paid tier. Use the picker above to choose a format and your child's age, customize the list in your browser, and print it straight to your home printer. The cheaper and easier a chart is to print, the more likely you are to actually restart it after a busy week, which is half the battle.

faq.q: What chores are appropriate for each age?
faq.a: As a rough ladder: toddlers and preschoolers focus on self-care and tidying their own things, and you should expect to redo the work. Through the elementary years kids can handle dishes, trash, simple cooking help, and yard jobs as their skill grows. Teens move to bigger, more independent responsibilities. Each age has its own chart linked below, built specifically for that stage, so pick your child's age to see the real list instead of guessing.

faq.q: Should I choose the chart by my child's age or their ability?
faq.a: Start with age to get a sensible baseline, then adjust for ability. If your child is brand new to chores, or a chart has flopped before, drop down a level so they can succeed every day, then raise it as the routine gets easy. We found a list a kid can consistently finish does far more for them than an ambitious one they quietly abandon — predictability is what makes the habit stick.

faq.q: Is a printable chart better than a chore app?
faq.a: For most families with younger kids, yes. The trouble with apps is that they live on a parent's phone, where the child never sees them, so they don't function as the visual reminder a chart is supposed to be. A printed sheet taped where the work happens stays in the kid's line of sight and quietly cues the next step. Apps can suit older, phone-owning teens, but for the years when a chart matters most, paper on the wall tends to win.
